title: Alembic migrations setup — non-blocking review follow-up
description: Non-blocking finding from pr-reviewer's review of PR #46 (db-migrations), tracked here per CLAUDE.md's autonomous-pipeline rule so it isn't lost once that PR merges.

checklist.step: docs/architecture/Backend.md §7 now correctly documents that `alembic stamp head` against a create_all-seeded database only produces a correct schema if that database's tables already match what the initial migration would create -- and flags that a database whose `positions` table predates `unique=True` being added to `PositionORM.ticker` (see api-portfolio-add-position's decisions) would get silently stamped as head without actually gaining that unique index, needing a manual fix-up migration instead. That caveat is documented but not defended against in tooling: nothing actually detects or fixes a drifted database at stamp time. Consider either (a) a small follow-up migration/script that idempotently ensures the unique index exists (e.g. `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`) so `stamp head` self-heals this specific known drift, or (b) a lightweight check (in the stamp-head docs workflow or a script) that compares the live schema against what the initial migration expects before stamping, so a drifted database fails loudly instead of silently passing. Low real-world likelihood in this single-developer MVP (no production deployment yet), which is why this is non-blocking rather than blocking the PR.

decisions.decision: Implemented option (a) from the checklist item (an idempotent fix-up so `stamp head` self-heals the known drift), as a standalone script `backend/scripts/fix_schema_drift.py` run before/after `alembic stamp head` rather than as either a normal Alembic revision or an env.py hook. It ensures `positions.ticker` has a unique index named `ix_positions_ticker`: no-op if the table doesn't exist yet or the index is already correct; drops and recreates the index as unique if a same-named non-unique index exists (the actual drifted shape — the column always had `index=True`, so the index exists under the same name before and after `unique=True` was added, which rules out `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` alone since SQLite's IF NOT EXISTS only checks the index name, not its definition); and lets the database's own constraint-violation error propagate (non-zero exit, explanatory stderr message) if duplicate ticker rows already exist under the old index, rather than swallowing it — that specific sub-case effectively also delivers option (b)'s 'fail loudly instead of silently stamping over a mismatch', for the one case where self-healing genuinely isn't safe (real duplicate data, not just a missing index).
decisions.rationale: Chose (a) over a pure (b) pre-stamp schema-diff check because a general schema-diff tool would be solving a broader problem than the one actually flagged (only positions.ticker's unique index is known to drift; every other column across positions/account/ohlcv_cache was introduced by the initial migration itself, so there's no pre-existing-database case for them to drift from) — a general diff check would need to enumerate and compare every table/column/index against what the initial migration produces, which is speculative work for drift that doesn't exist yet, whereas a narrow, self-healing fix-up directly resolves the one concrete case the review flagged, in the same amount of code, without requiring an operator to read a failure message and go figure out the fix by hand. Rejected embedding the fix inside app/db/migrations/env.py (e.g. gated on the alembic command being 'stamp') because env.py runs for every alembic invocation (upgrade, revision --autogenerate, etc.), and silently mutating the schema as a side effect of an unrelated command (or making env.py's behavior depend on which subcommand invoked it) is a more surprising, harder-to-test place for this than an explicit, separately-run script documented right next to the `alembic stamp head` instruction it's paired with. Rejected making it a normal Alembic revision (chained after the initial migration) because that doesn't actually work for this use case: `stamp head` records a revision as applied without executing it, so a later revision that 'fixes' the index would never run against a database that gets stamped straight to head — the whole point of self-healing at stamp time requires code that runs outside the normal migration-execution path, which is what a standalone script provides. Verified this script doesn't just no-op on the common case: added backend/tests/integration/test_fix_schema_drift.py covering (1) no positions table yet, (2) the drifted shape (non-unique same-named index, reproduced with raw SQL matching the pre-unique=True model) both freshly fixed and idempotently re-run, (3) the genuine-duplicate-data case failing loudly and leaving the table untouched (no partial index, no dropped rows), (4) a database already correct (create_all with the current model) staying a no-op, and (5) an end-to-end fix-then-stamp-then-upgrade-head sequence against a throwaway SQLite file, following the same real-subprocess pattern db-migrations.json's own test_db_migrations.py already established. This is code-now, not documentation-only: single-developer MVP with no production DB deployed yet (per the PR #46 review notes) means low near-term likelihood, but the fix is small (~60 lines), fully self-contained, doesn't touch the coverage gate (backend/scripts/ was already outside pyproject.toml's `source = ["app"]`, same as the pre-existing scripts/export_openapi.py), and directly removes the operator-must-have-read-the-doc dependency the review flagged as the actual gap — documentation alone leaves the exact same silent-drift risk the review called out, just with a paragraph explaining it after the fact.
